body:
![high](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/high-priority.svg)

There are two critical issues in the current runner exit and duration handling:

1. **Race Condition on Successful Runs**: If the runner exits successfully (exit code `0`), the script still proceeds to send a failure diagnostic. Because the controller's monitoring loop checks for the failure file before GitHub's API updates the run status to `completed` (which is subject to API latency), successful runs will be erroneously flagged as failures. We should exit cleanly with `0` if `runner_exit` is `0`.
2. **Clock Drift Validation Failure**: The duration calculation can yield a negative value if clock synchronization occurs during VM startup. A negative duration will fail the controller's strict validation (`(int)durationValue < 0`), rejecting the diagnostic and causing the pilot to hang for 65 minutes instead of failing fast. We should clamp the duration to `[0, 86400]`.

```suggestion
runner_exit=$?
set -e
runner_duration=$(( $(date +%s) - runner_started_at ))
if [ "${runner_duration}" -lt 0 ]; then
  runner_duration=0
elif [ "${runner_duration}" -gt 86400 ]; then
  runner_duration=86400
fi

if [ "${runner_exit}" -eq 0 ]; then
  rm -f "${runner_log}"
  exit 0
fi
```

body:
![medium](https://www.gstatic.com/codereviewagent/medium-priority.svg)

The `HttpListener` in `CIEPRServices.cs` registers the prefix with a trailing slash (`http://172.31.154.1:9443/bootstrap-ack/`). Sending a request to `http://172.31.154.1:9443/bootstrap-ack` (without the trailing slash) can cause HTTP.sys to issue a redirect or fail to match. Since `curl` is run with `--fail` but without `-L` (to follow redirects), this can cause the diagnostic upload to fail silently. Adding the trailing slash ensures a direct, reliable match.

```suggestion
curl --fail --silent --show-error --max-time 10 \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "${diagnostic}" \
  http://172.31.154.1:9443/bootstrap-ack/ || true
```

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Avoid reporting successful runner exits as failures**

For a single-use JIT runner, `run.sh` can exit normally after it finishes its one job, but this block posts a bootstrap failure for every exit, including `runner_exit=0`. The pilot then treats the resulting `.failure.json` as fatal whenever the Actions run has not yet appeared as `completed`, so a successful job can be marked failed if the GitHub run-status read lags the runner process exit; only early/nonzero startup exits should create this diagnostic.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Bind failure records to the admitted VM**

Because the bootstrap endpoint remains reachable from the guest after the candidate workflow starts, any process on `172.31.154.10` can POST this exact failure schema with arbitrary GUIDs and this line will persist unbounded `.failure.json` files without checking an active/admitted VM or that `runner_name` matches `vm_uuid`. A malicious or runaway job can therefore pollute/fill the protected ACK directory, and can also overwrite the current VM's diagnostic; validate against the existing admission/current-run binding before writing evidence.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Bound the diagnostic log to startup only**

Redirecting the entire `run.sh` process to `/run/cie-jit/runner-start.log` means that once the runner successfully connects and executes the dispatched job, the file can contain the candidate workflow's console output for the whole run, not just startup diagnostics. A verbose or secret-printing job can therefore leave workflow output in the guest until exit and potentially fill `/run`; cap the capture and stop/delete it once startup succeeds instead of logging the whole runner lifetime.
